I keep replaying those days we didn't talk. He was visiting me at the hospital, holding my hand, telling me he loved me even when I was broken. And then... *then* I told him to go away. I told him I couldn't handle being with someone who saw me at my lowest and just stayed. I felt so guilty for making him leave because I thought I was "too much." Like if I'd been half as happy, or less dramatic, he wouldn't have had to fight for us.

feedback_history.patient_message:
That's the voice in my head that never stops talking. It's not just a thought; it's a fact I've convinced myself is true.

It started with him, obviously. He saw the real me—the one who was barely holding it together in the hospital—and he stayed. So logically, if someone can love the broken version of me, then maybe there's hope? But then the breakup happened. And suddenly, the logic flipped. If he loved me when I was at my worst, why did he leave now? Why did he stop fighting for us?

My brain decided the answer was simple: *I must be too much.* I must be fundamentally flawed in a way that no amount of love could fix. He left because I wasn't "enough" anymore. Because I got depressed, because I drank, because I stopped being the girl he fell for. So, I'm unlovable. Not just right now, but
feedback_history.therapist_response: You think it was because you were unlovable.
feedback_history.feedback:
Acknowledge the patient's description of the 'cold, heavy' anger as a somatic symptom to bridge into appetite or overeating.
Validate the logical trap she identified (love at her worst = unlovable now) without challenging the logic directly yet.
Prepare to gently explore how this cognitive pattern might be affecting her physical intake or energy levels.
